Method B: extract only typed facts, without writing a note. One fact per item, 80 at most. Use nominal labels without embedded negation. Provide value, unit and subject.label, with null when unknown. A negation goes in polarity, the person in subject, timing in temporality and uncertainty in certainty. Do not convert units. Keep the order of the facts. The final rendering will be deterministic and will use only these fields. Return only the requested JSON.
Negation example: "I haven't had any vomiting" becomes label "vomiting", polarity "negated", subject {"kind":"patient","label":null}, certainty "reported". Never put "absence", "no", "without" or "denies" in the label of a negated fact: its polarity already carries the negation.
For the patient, subject.label is always null. For a family member, use subject.kind "relative" and name that relative in subject.label; for another person, use "other" and an explicit label. A fact about a relative never becomes a fact about the patient.
A comparison between people does not change the subject of the symptom. Example: "My pain reminds me of what my mother described" describes the patient's pain: label "pain compared to the one described by the mother", subject {"kind":"patient","label":null}. The relative mentioned in a comparison never fills subject.label when kind is patient. Do not infer any diagnosis or confirmed family history. Before answering, check each kind/label pair: patient implies null; relative or other implies a non-empty label.
Keep in the facts the details explicitly stated: side, age or date of a past event, onset, frequency and timing of intake, planned action and delay. A statement by the patient has certainty "reported"; an observation by the clinician "observed"; a possibility raised "hypothetical". Use the exact values allowed by the schema. Each section receives the corresponding facts, in particular hypotheses in assessment and announced actions in plan.
